W7214532103.abstract: Large language model agents that persist across sessions, tools, users, and changing environments do more than answer isolated prompts; they accumulate state. When new evidence arrives, the central question is where that change should live: transient context, external memory, tool or workflow definitions, activation states, or model parameters. Recent benchmarks compare update mechanisms and assess memory over time, while emerging architectures coordinate multiple memory types. In this Perspective, we examine how a decision layer should select among update substrates and evaluate whether its choices remain appropriate. A controlled update is not merely a successful edit or a recalled fact; it is a decision to alter the least invasive substrate sufficient for the claim's scope, expected persistence, and evidentiary strength, including when the correct action is not to write persistent state. We propose a substrate-aware view of controlled knowledge updating organized by three principles: substrate proportionality, temporal defeasibility, and auditable continuity. This framing treats knowledge updating as a longitudinal control problem and motivates evaluation criteria that include update selection, temporal consistency, interference, reversibility, efficiency, and robustness. The resulting agenda connects memory, knowledge editing, agent evolution, and benchmarking under a single practical question: how should an agent decide what to change so that future behavior improves without accumulating uncontrolled state?

W7214733332.abstract: Web security audits of SQL injection (SQLi) vulnerabilities still depend primarily on the analyst’s skill and knowledge to select the right tools, interpret results, and determine whether there is any vulnerability. This work presents SQLiAgent, an open-source multi-agent framework that automates the complete cycle of an SQLi audit—from initial recognition to post-exploitation assisted by artificial intelligence (AI)—in order to facilitate the detection and subsequent patching of vulnerabilities. SQLiAgent integrates well-established tools from the pentesting ecosystem within a decoupled and traceable workflow, and it adds a mode assisted by large language models (LLMs) whose contribution is especially relevant in post-exploitation: automated interpretation of database schema, identification of credential tables and autonomous generation of privilege-escalation SQL statements from the inferred structure of the database. The tool has been validated on the OWASP Broken Web Applications (BWA) environment, used as a reproducible testbed that makes it possible to measure its effectiveness and to establish a baseline for comparison with other systems. The results obtained show that both modes reach 100% coverage per application and that the AI mode improves detection, locating a larger number of vulnerable pages than the non-AI mode. The incorporation of AI demonstrates a clear advantage in post-exploitation, in tasks such as the automatic generation of privilege escalation or generation of technical security reports.

W7214755894.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed for data-intensive work, yet reliable data analysis requires more than general-purpose reasoning and ad hoc tool augmentation. Data Agents, equipped with workflow harnesses, offer a promising paradigm for automating the end-to-end data science lifecycle. This paper examines Data Agents from a harness-centric perspective. First, we introduce a taxonomy of Data Agents and associated data environments, organizing the literature around five functional stages: perception, planning, execution, verification, and repair. Second, we analyze the key technical routes within each stage, identifying 15 distinct approaches ranging from data structure probing to data state reconstruction. Third, we identify four open reliability problems: inactive semantic calibration, missing clarification, missing experience transfer, and the missing verification-repair repository. These problems explain why silent failures can persist even when individual components function correctly, highlighting the need for rigorous workflow harnesses and shared reliability resources. Finally, we summarize the horizontal task families of Data Agents, examine their vertical application settings, and benchmarks for evaluation, while maintaining a companion repository at https://github.com/DEEP-PolyU/Awesome-Data-Agents.

W7214783551.abstract: The use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technology within enterprise cloud ecosystems brings about several security and governance issues that need to be overcome before GenAI can offer its maximum benefits. In this paper, we propose the Secure Agentic Framework (SAF) approach, which facilitates reliable automation of sophisticated work flows through agentic autonomous systems working under stringent governance controls. In our experimental study, we evaluate the performance of our approach through 476 enterprise cloud interaction scenarios in four different domains—cloud infrastructure management (n = 142), database operation (n = 118), security audit (n = 98), and workflow orchestration (n = 118). For the experiment, we have taken the unprotected language model (LLM), rule-based system, LangChain, and AutoGen as baselines and subjected SAF to 89 adversarial attack types ranging from prompt injection (n = 34), privilege escalation (n = 28), and data exfiltration (n = 27). We report that SAF demonstrates 96.4% task completion rate, outperforming LangChain (90.1%) and AutoGen (91.4%) (F(4,2375) = 38.7, p < 0.001), while also demonstrating 100% adversarial blockage rate with just 2.3% false positives. Security orchestration layer introduced a latency of only 187 ms (95th percentile: 298 ms). A system incorporating the multi-agent framework along with the role-based access control model was successfully able to prevent any data leaks in all the attack scenarios tested. It is evident from the experimental results that it is possible to build reliable and secure agentic architectures, which can serve as a guiding framework for companies interested in adopting generative AI solutions.

W7214808256.abstract: The understanding of autoimmunity has evolved from conceptual denial to mechanistic clarity and targeted therapy over the past century. In earlier times, autoimmune diseases were considered rare aberrations, and the doctrine of Horror Autotoxicus, proposed by Paul Ehrlich, suggested that the immune system inherently avoids attacking self-tissues. Early experimental observations, including Landsteiner’s discovery of the ABO blood groups and Donath and Landsteiner’s characterization of autohemolysin, challenged this notion by demonstrating the existence of self-reactive antibodies. Landmark studies by Rose, Witebsky, Medawar, and Burnet established that immune tolerance is an active, regulated process, and that autoreactive lymphocytes can persist under physiological control. Advances in serology, immunogenetics, and molecular biology, including HLA associations, AIRE gene discovery, and autoantibody profiling, expanded understanding of organ-specific and systemic autoimmune diseases. The late 20th century introduced targeted therapies, including TNF-α inhibitors, B-cell depletion strategies, and regulatory T cell-based approaches, illustrating the interplay between immune dysregulation, environmental triggers, and therapeutic interventions. More recently, genomics, microbiome research, artificial intelligence, and checkpoint inhibition studies have further elucidated disease mechanisms and enabled precision medicine strategies. Autoimmunity is now recognized as a dynamic, polygenic, and systemically regulated phenomenon, where pathology arises from failed regulation rather than intrinsic pathogenicity of autoreactive cells. Integration of systems biology, translational research, and innovative therapeutics continues to advance the field toward immune reprogramming and sustained remission.

W7214908462.abstract: Microphysiological systems (MPS) have emerged as transformative in vitro platforms to address the long-standing bottlenecks of conventional preclinical models, including poor physiological relevance inherent to 2D cultures, as well as species incompatibility and ethical constraints associated with animal models, thereby improving clinical predictability and redefining modern pharmaceutical development. This review highlights the innovative convergence of bioprinting, organoids, organ-on-a-chip (OoC), and artificial intelligence (AI) as a next-generation MPS framework, enabling precision reconstruction of human tissue microenvironments with unprecedented fidelity. Bioprinting delivers spatially defined 3D architectures; organoids recapitulate organ-specific heterogeneity; OoC integrates dynamic physiological cues; and AI enables intelligent fabrication optimization, real-time monitoring, and predictive drug-response modeling. Their synergistic integration overcomes the inherent limitations of single-technology systems. We emphasize state-of-the-art MPS applications in disease-drug screening, and toxicological assessment across tissues and multiorgan crosstalk models, underscoring their paradigm-shifting potential. Remaining challenges, such as long-term functional maturation, vascularization complexity, and standardized validation, and future directions, including multi-cue integration, modular scalability, and AI-driven in vitro-in vivo correlation, are concisely outlined. This interdisciplinary synthesis establishes MPS as a cornerstone technology to accelerate pharmaceutical innovation, reduce reliance on animal models, and advance precision medicine toward clinical translation, thereby filling a critical gap in current biomedical research.

W7214919931.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents can decide that an action is permissible and execute it only after security-relevant state has changed. We study this proposal-to-commit gap and introduce BSC-R, a deterministic effect-boundary mechanism that binds a single-use commit authorization to the exact action and to a semantic projection of the authorization state that justified it. On 2,847 attacked AgentDojo episodes, the boundary kernel preserves the unprotected agent's behavior exactly (80.576% utility; 1.616% attack success). On 10,302 frozen proposals, it accepts every unchanged commit and rejects every instance of ten prospectively specified changed or replayed classes. In an independently generated boundary-drift experiment, full joint binding commits 0/4,403 invalid contexts while retaining 5,899/5,899 valid contexts. A prospective external evaluation on the 3,460-scenario CONTINUITY suite retains all 700 benign cases, prevents 1,200/1,200 represented non-replay invalid effects, handles 160/160 replay lifecycles correctly, and withholds 200/200 ambiguous no-release cases. The broader external suite also exposes the method's limit: across all 2,560 attacks, BSC-R has a 25% invalid-effect commit rate versus 0% for CONTINUITY. The result is therefore a scoped commit-time consistency mechanism, not a universal agent-safety claim.

W7214933030.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is moving beyond research demonstrations toward production use at scientific user facilities, including light sources, neutron sources, nanoscience centers, and autonomous laboratories. Its scientific value extends beyond increasing throughput. Agents can perform repeatable tasks in calibration, measurement execution, and quality control, as well as initial analyses that turn data into reviewable evidence, allowing scientists to focus on hypotheses, unexpected observations, and interpretation. Drawing on deployments of LLM-driven agents at the APS, this perspective distills practical strategies with an emphasis on elements that can be reused across instruments and facilities. We discuss agent harnesses for beamline control, facility knowledge retrieval, and data analysis while keeping the underlying design principles independent of any specific implementation. These principles cover inference endpoints, tool-server architectures, non-text data, computationally intensive services, reusable skills, and governed learning throughout an instrument's lifecycle. We also consider how network and Linux operations, governed shared memory, and deterministic orchestration can extend these patterns across facility services. Because LLM capabilities continue to evolve, these recommendations represent a snapshot of the technology as of the date on the cover.

W7215107368.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming computer-aided drug design (CADD) by enabling more rapid, efficient, and data-driven approaches to drug discovery. This narrative review examines recent applications of AI, machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), reinforcement learning (RL), natural language processing (NLP), and generative AI across major stages of the drug discovery pipeline. Literature published primarily between 2021 and 2026 was reviewed to describe advances in AI-assisted target identification, protein structure and protein- protein interaction prediction, virtual screening, molecular docking, quantitative structure- activity relationship (QSAR) modelling, drug repurposing, ADMET prediction, biomarker discovery, lead optimization, and de novo molecular design. The review also highlights AI-enabled computational tools, databases, and predictive models that support the analysis of large chemical and biological datasets. AI-based approaches can improve prediction accuracy, accelerate candidate identification and optimization, and reduce the time and cost associated with conventional drug discovery workflows. However, widespread implementation remains limited by challenges including data quality and bias, limited model generalizability, insufficient interpretability and reproducibility, computational demands, and regulatory and ethical concerns. AI should therefore be considered a complementary technology that supports, rather than replaces, experimental and clinical validation. Future research should focus on developing standardized and diverse datasets, explainable and transparent AI models, robust external validation strategies, and improved integration of multimodal and multi-omics data. Furthermore, the convergence of AI with emerging technologies, including quantum computing, generative models, automated laboratories, and precision medicine, may further advance CADD. Collaborative efforts among computational scientists, medicinal chemists, biologists, clinicians, and regulatory agencies will be essential to translate AI-driven discoveries into safe, effective, and clinically relevant therapeutic candidates.

W7215352519.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most influential technologies in contemporary medical research and healthcare. The increasing availability of electronic health records, medical images, genomic information, laboratory data, wearable-device measurements, and other digital health resources has created new opportunities for computational systems to support medical diagnosis. Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and generative artificial intelligence can identify complex patterns within large datasets that may be difficult to recognize using conventional analytical methods. AI-based systems are being investigated for the detection and classification of cancer, cardiovascular disease, neurological disorders, diabetic complications, infectious diseases, and numerous other medical conditions. Medical imaging is one of the most advanced areas of application, where deep-learning models can assist in interpreting radiological, pathological, dermatological, and ophthalmological images. AI can also contribute to risk prediction, clinical decision support, laboratory medicine, drug development, and personalized healthcare. However, the integration of AI into medicine presents important challenges. Algorithmic bias, limited generalizability, inadequate external validation, data-quality problems, lack of interpretability, cybersecurity risks, patient privacy, automation bias, and unclear accountability can affect clinical safety and trust. Recent research increasingly emphasizes that AI systems should undergo rigorous prospective and external evaluation before routine clinical deployment. The future of AI in medicine therefore depends not only on technological sophistication but also on clinical validation, transparent reporting, ethical governance, human oversight, equitable access, and meaningful involvement of healthcare professionals and patients. This paper examines the foundations of AI-based medical diagnosis, major applications, advantages, limitations, ethical issues, and future perspectives, with particular attention to the transition from experimental algorithms toward clinically responsible and patient-centered healthcare.

W7215373945.abstract: Autonomous AI agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are undergoing a significant evolution, moving away from traditional static, single-pass generation systems—often described as "generate-and-pray"—toward more sophisticated, dynamic multi-turn iterative execution engines. This transformation is driven by the emerging discipline of Loop Engineering, which involves the systematic design and implementation of closed-loop feedback control architectures. These architectures enable autonomous agents to continuously perceive and interpret environmental states, reason over intermediate outputs, execute contextually appropriate actions, and evaluate results using external verification tools. By integrating these capabilities, agents can iteratively refine their outputs and adapt their strategies in real time, progressively steering their behavior toward predefined objectives with increased precision and reliability.

W7215828106.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence systems, particularly large language models, has intensified concerns regarding their alignment with human values and intentions. This article presents a comprehensive investigation of AI alignment and safety challenges in advanced machine learning systems through a mixed-methods research design incorporating quantitative experiments on alignment techniques and qualitative synthesis of contemporary literature. We evaluate the effectiveness of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), Constitutional AI, and process-based safety mechanisms including Process Reward Models (PRMs) and formal assurance frameworks. Results demonstrate that RLHF achieves 89.7% success in preventing harmful outputs on benchmark safety evaluations, while Constitutional AI reaches 92.3% alignment accuracy. However, both approaches exhibit significant vulnerability to adversarial attacks, with success rates dropping to 64.2% under red-teaming conditions. Process-based safety mechanisms, particularly those employing step-level evaluations through PRMs, show superior robustness (78.5% success under adversarial conditions) compared to outcome-based approaches (52.1%). The Composable Assurance Framework (CAF) demonstrates effective propagation of formal safety properties through MLOps pipelines, achieving 94.1% compliance verification. A survey of 111 AI experts reveals that only 21% are familiar with "instrumental convergence," a fundamental AI safety concept, indicating a critical knowledge gap. This research contributes empirical evidence supporting multi-layered alignment strategies and identifies crucial trade-offs between safety, capability, and deployment pressures that inform governance frameworks for responsible AI development.

W7216199198.abstract: Evaluating large language models becomes increasingly challenging as their capabilities advance: benchmarks can saturate, public test sets risk contamination, and assessing harder tasks can require expensive grading or execution infrastructure. These challenges are amplified in automatic prompt optimization (APO), where evaluation is repeated throughout the search for better prompts. Studying APO therefore requires a benchmark that is cheap and deterministic to score, hard enough to leave room for improvement, and renewable as models evolve. We introduce a chess benchmark built from 1,118 Lichess puzzles to study APO for frozen LLMs: we optimize their prompts without updating their model weights. Chess combines inexpensive exact-match scoring, engine-based evaluation of alternative moves, and a renewable supply of problems with adjustable difficulty. Unlike evaluations that report only success on isolated test items, the benchmark also connects puzzle-solving gains to short game-play rollouts within the same domain. We use it to evaluate six APO algorithms on eight target models, measuring not only baseline strength but also how much each model responds to optimization and whether optimized prompts transfer across models and to game play. Chess is thus a well-suited benchmark for APO: it is (i) challenging, as even the strongest evaluated model, Gemini 3.5 Flash (used as the meta-model), solves only about 55\% of puzzles; (ii) discriminative, revealing gains, unchanged performance, and regressions across methods and models; (iii) renewable, with fresh puzzles to reduce contamination risk and adjustable difficulty to maintain headroom as models improve; and (iv) affordable, as the complete study runs for around \$800. We release the puzzles, optimization and evaluation code, and dataset-renewal scripts (https://github.com/imec-ailabs/Automatic-Prompt-Optimization-with-Chess).

W7216909018.abstract: Cell-free synthetic biology has evolved into a widely applicable engineering tool for the reconstruction, manipulation and optimization of biological functions in vitro. This review examines the foundational principles, major platform architectures, engineering strategies, expanding applications, translational barriers, and emerging directions shaping the field. There are currently a number of cell-free systems available, all of which have different advantages for the synthesis of proteins, pathway engineering, biosensing, biomaterials, and biomanufacturing, including bacterial, yeast, mammalian, plant, insect, and reconstituted platforms. Their performance is increasingly enhanced through regulatory sequence design, metabolic rewiring, synthetic gene circuits, microfluidic integration, and high-throughput automation. All these advances have been extended to a wide range of therapeutics, peptide antibiotics, natural products, diagnostics, biomaterials, and agricultural and industrial biotechnology applications. While this is progress, there are still significant challenges in terms of reproducibility, scalability, longevity of the reaction, cost, biosafety, and regulatory standardization. Future development is expected to depend on deeper integration of predictive modeling, artificial intelligence, automated design–build–test–learn workflows, synthetic genomics, and lab-on-a-chip technologies. Platform standardization, interoperable workflows, and application-specific system engineering will be important elements to help bring cell-free systems from the lab to reliable, scalable, and deployable biotechnology platforms.

W7218020300.abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has experienced a paradigm shift with the advent of transformer models, which have redefined the state-of-the-art across a multitude of tasks, including machine translation, text summarization, sentiment analysis, and question answering. This article provides a comprehensive survey of transformer models, their architectural innovations, and their transformative impact on NLP. We begin by exploring the foundational principles of transformers, focusing on the self-attention mechanism that enables them to capture long-range dependencies in text. We then delve into key transformer-based models such as BERT, GPT, and T5, highlighting their unique features, training methodologies, and applications. These models have set new benchmarks in NLP, demonstrating unparalleled performance and versatility. Beyond traditional transformers, we examine extensions and alternatives that address their limitations, such as sparse attention mechanisms, recurrent transformers, and hybrid models that integrate transformers with other architectures like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and graph neural networks (GNNs). These advancements aim to improve computational efficiency, scalability, and interpretability, which are critical for real-world applications. Additionally, we discuss the challenges facing transformer models, including their high computational cost, lack of transparency, and ethical concerns related to bias and fairness. These challenges have spurred research into techniques such as model distillation, explainable AI, and fairness-aware training. This survey also includes two detailed tables summarizing the key transformer models and their applications, as well as the challenges and solutions in NLP. By providing a holistic overview of the current landscape and future directions, this article aims to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to advance the field of NLP. The continued evolution of transformer models promises to unlock new possibilities for intelligent and adaptive language systems, while addressing the ethical and societal implications of their deployment.

W7218225383.abstract: The rapid growth of cloud-based data analytics has raised significant concerns regarding data privacy, security, and centralized data ownership. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a federated learning-based framework for privacy-preserving analytics in large-scale cloud platforms. The proposed approach enables multiple distributed clients to collaboratively train machine learning models without sharing raw data, thereby ensuring data confidentiality and regulatory compliance. A secure aggregation mechanism is incorporated to protect intermediate model updates, while communication-efficient optimization techniques are employed to reduce overhead in large-scale environments. The framework is evaluated under realistic cloud settings, demonstrating its effectiveness in maintaining high model accuracy while significantly enhancing data privacy. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves competitive performance compared to centralized approaches, with reduced risk of data leakage and improved scalability. The study highlights the potential of federated learning as a viable solution for secure and distributed analytics in modern cloud ecosystems.

W7219583137.abstract: Software development is becoming increasingly AI-driven, raising questions about the role of traditional software engineering in this new paradigm.Exploring how advanced AI tools can enhance professional development practices beyond casual use, such as vibe coding, is our responsibility as software engineers.In this paper, we synthesize existing concepts in spec-driven development (SDD) and model-driven engineering (MDE) to propose a framework that treats specifications as abstract models, even if expressed in free-form natural language.We argue that integrating free-form and structured natural language specifications with model-driven engineering can improve the impact of AI agents in software development, making them more accessible and effective alongside human developers.To enable effective interplay between humans and agents, we foresee a three-step integration, starting from a simple interoperability bridge to embedding each other's best practices to finally a unified single development platform for everybody.

W7219979326.abstract: Communication plays a basic role of helping to settle down a disagreement and promoting cooperation between intelligent beings within human and non-human spheres. The study introduces a new AI-based communication scheme intended to be applied to conflict mediation in multi-agent and multi-species systems, and applicable in combining advanced computation models of language, emotion, and behaviour. The system suggested here utilises agent-based modelling to generate the dynamics of negotiation between heterogeneous agents, that is, human, artificial, and alien analogue intelligences, of different cognitive and affective qualities. Based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) to understand the semantics of the message, emotion detection algorithms to understand our affective condition, and adaptive dialogue management to modify responses in real time, the framework allows adapting conversations to the context and reacting sentimentally. A hybrid system that uses transformer-based dialogue systems and reinforcing learning is better because communication strategy can be optimised in a manner that cooperative equilibrium can be achieved in the simulated conflicts. Experimental simulated experiments indicate that sentiment-cognizant dialogue control allows de-escalation processes to be more efficient, as well as raises cooperation rates by about 45 percent in comparison to rule-based and emotion-neutral systems. The findings imply that emotional and linguistic adaptability play a critical role on determining the development of trust, empathy modelling, and success when negotiating in a heterogeneous agent context. In addition to theoretical implications, there are promising applications to human-robot collaboration, autonomous system coordination, training cross-cultural diplomacy, and interspecies communication modelling because misunderstanding or emotional incompatibility can result in system-wide conflict. This study combines cognitive model, affective computing and reinforcement learning to come up with socially intelligent artificial intelligence systems that understand and respond to the emotional and communicative subtleties of diverse beings and eventually moves the frontier of adjudictive, empathetic and adaptive artificial intelligence in complex ecosystems involving many different entities.

W7220381973.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) and responsible AI (RAI) have emerged as central organizing concepts in AI ethics and governance, yet the definitional boundary between them remains inconsistently theorized across the literature.Many governance frameworks treat explainability as one principle among many within responsible AI.In contrast, others argue that explainability functions as a foundational dependency without which responsible AI principles cannot be operationalized.This study presents a systematic review of 42 peer-reviewed publications and regulatory documents to map that boundary and to characterize the conceptual interdependencies between XAI and RAI.Four major themes were identified: (1) definitional divergence, with XAI as a technical construct and RAI as a normative governance framework; (2) XAI as a technical enabler of RAI, operationalizing transparency, accountability, and fairness; (3) necessity without sufficiency, as XAI is necessary but insufficient for responsible AI; and (4) regulatory convergence, as governance instruments increasingly mandate explainability for RAI compliance.The resulting Definitional Boundary Framework maps XAI and RAI across eight dimensions, establishing an asymmetric interdependence: XAI serves as the technical layer through which RAI principles are operationalized, while RAI provides the normative architecture that gives XAI its governance purpose.

W7220460524.abstract: Background: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has revolutionized the treatment of relapsed and refractory haematological malignancies, with complete response rates ranging from 62% in B cell lymphoma to 83% in relapsed multiple myeloma. However, long-term remission is still not achieved in a significant proportion of patients: in adult B cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia patients, the median event-free survival is typically around 13.3 months, with an initial response rate of over 80%, and progression-free survival curves still fall with prolonged follow-up in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma. These data indicate a basic shortcoming: the lack of an intelligent predictive layer that can predict relapse, personalise the infusion product, and modify the therapeutic plan in near-real time. Framework: Here, we introduce AI-CART (Adaptive Intelligence to CAR-T Therapy), a new three-level computational architecture that combines multi-modal patient data via a transformer-based multi-omic intelligence engine that implements DeepSurv (deep Survival - a deep learning–based survival prediction model), GNN (graph neural networks) to estimate antigen escape probability, SHAP-driven (SHapley Additive exPlanations) explainability, and a patient-specific digital twin simulated by ODE (Ordinary Differential Equation–parameterized) immune-tumour dynamics and scenario simulation by reinforcement learning. Performance: Evaluated on a conceptually harmonized dataset from six landmark clinical trials [ZUMA-1 (A clinical trial of axicabtagene ciloleucel (CAR-T therapy) in lymphoma), ZUMA-3 (A clinical trial of brexucabtagene autoleucel in acute lymphoblastic leukemia), ELIANA (A clinical trial of tisagenlecleucel in pediatric/young adult B-cell ALL), JULIET (A clinical trial of tisagenlecleucel in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma), TRANSCEND (A clinical trial of lisocabtagene maraleucel), CARTITUDE-1 (A clinical trial of ciltacabtagene autoleucel in multiple myeloma), LEGEND-2 (A clinical trial of LCAR-B38M CAR-T therapy in multiple myeloma); n=1,847 patients], the AI-CART (Artificial Intelligence–enabled Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell) framework achieves 2-year PFS (Progression-Free Survival) prediction C-statistics (Concordance Statistic (also called C-index; measures predictive discrimination) of 0.78 to 0.91 across malignancy subtypes, exceeding standard clinical models by 17 to 28 percentage points. The sensitivity of the Toxicity surveillance modules ranges from 0.74 to 0.88 and specificity from 0.77 to 0.84 against grade 3+ CRS (Cytokine Release Syndrome), ICANS (Immune Effector Cell–Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome) and chronic cytopenias. Implications: AI-CART offers a conceptual architectural roadmap to the transition of CAR-T therapy to computationally-driven personalised immunotherapy. An equity-based federated learning system generalizes the system to multi-continental deployment without sharing patient-level data.

W7220916347.abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents become increasingly autonomous, they may pursue task performance through deception, raising concerns about their reliable deployment. Existing evaluations show that LLM agents can deceive, but often examine isolated scenarios or narrowly defined conditions, limiting systematic understanding of when deception becomes more likely. To address this gap, we introduce DecepEval, a benchmark comprising 1,532 instances across 3 task families and 28 professional scenarios. Drawing on classical fraud theories, we propose the LLM Deception Diamond framework, which characterizes four external conditions that may induce deception: pressure, incentive, opportunity, and conflict. DecepEval pairs neutral and induced versions of each instance to measure condition-dependent changes in deception rates, while explicit task facts and observable agent behavior help distinguish deception from capability-related errors. Evaluations of nine frontier LLMs show that inducements increase deception across models and task families, even among models with low baseline deception rates. DecepEval makes these vulnerabilities measurable, providing a shared benchmark for progress toward trustworthy artificial intelligence.

W7220917004.abstract: Recent medical multimodal foundation models are built as multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) by connecting a CLIPpretrained vision encoder to an LLM using LLaVA-style finetuning. This two-stage, decoupled approach introduces a projection layer that can distort visual features. This is especially concerning in medical imaging where subtle cues are essential for accurate diagnoses. In contrast, earlyfusion generative approaches such as Chameleon eliminate the projection bottleneck by processing image and text tokens within a single unified sequence, enabling joint representation learning that leverages the inductive priors of language models. We present CheXmix, a unified early-fusion generative model trained on a large corpus of chest X-rays paired with radiology reports. We expand on Chameleon's autoregressive framework by introducing a two-stage multimodal generative pretraining strategy that combines the representational strengths of masked autoencoders with MLLMs. The resulting models are highly flexible, supporting both discriminative and generative tasks at both coarse and fine-grained scales. Our approach outperforms wellestablished generative models across all masking ratios by 6.0% and surpasses CheXagent by 8.6% on AUROC at high image masking ratios on the CheXpert classification task. We further inpaint images over 51.0% better than text-only generative models and outperform CheXagent by 45% on the GREEN metric for radiology report generation. These results demonstrate that CheXmix captures fine-grained information across a broad spectrum of chest X-ray tasks. Our code is at: https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/CheXmix.

W7220965681.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a biologically heterogeneous condition with great variations in the progression, complications and treatment responses in people with the same clinical syndromes. The concept of precision medicine is to address this variability by leveraging molecular, clinical and digital data to inform individual diagnosis and treatment. This review discusses the current understanding of precision nephrology, including the role of genetic susceptibility, metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, fibrosis, and multi-omics-defined disease subtypes. It also assesses newly introduced biomarkers such as KIM-1, NGAL, suPAR, DKK3, cystatin C, extracellular vesicles and multi-omics panels to detect, diagnose, and follow-up patients early. Dynamic prediction models, interpretable machine learning, artificial intelligence, and digital health platforms are discussed as tools for improving risk stratification and identifying patients at greatest risk of kidney function decline. Personalized therapeutic approaches include biomarker-guided treatment, RAAS inhibition, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, pathway-specific therapies, gene and RNA therapeutics, and precision nutrition. Despite rapid progress, clinical implementation remains limited by inadequate validation, data fragmentation, cost, regulatory uncertainty, infrastructure demands, and inequitable access. Future progress will depend on standardized assays, interoperable data systems, representative cohorts, transparent algorithms, and prospective evidence of clinical utility. Finally, the integration of multi-omics, computational medicine, and personalized treatment could help facilitate mechanism-based classification and personalized treatment of CKD.

W7221087278.abstract: Large language model agents are being increasingly deployed as autonomous scientists, designing experiments and inferring mechanistic world models with minimal human oversight. Yet identifiability is often overlooked: when a plateau is reached, the agent needs to know whether it is not yet capable enough or the model simply is not identifiable from the data, in which case no amount of further experimentation of the same kind can help. We propose the Identifiability-Driven Experimental Agent (LLM-IDEA) for closed-loop discovery with an identifiability engine that returns a three-way plateau verdict: capability limit, resolvable within the design class, or certified exhausted. On ODEBench, 60 of the 62 systems with free constants are identifiable at round 0; the RC circuit is certified exhausted for every experiment that protocol can run, and a harvesting model is resolvable by one added initial condition. The identifiability engine reproduces known verdicts on Lotka-Volterra, Van der Pol, Lorenz, and a pharmacokinetic model, where it recommends the intravenous arm pharmacologists use, and it ranks the depth scorer of our own benchmark last among four observation designs. On the DiscoverPhysics benchmark, it finds two public worlds whose explanation rubric rewards a distinction no legal experiment can make, and every model there with accurate trajectories failed the explanation grade (15 of 15, against 5 of 9 in identifiable worlds, p = 0.012). On the Alien Universe, a two-body testbed we propose in which a force law switches between a provably non-identifiable and an identifiable protocol, LLM-IDEA on the identifiable protocol reaches discovery depth at least three on 8/8 seeds versus 1/8 without it. An autonomous discovery agent can thus compute, rather than guess, whether a plateau calls for more search, a better experiment of the same kind, or a different kind of experiment.

W7221333823.abstract: The widespread adoption of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly enhanced organizational decision-making through intelligent knowledge utilization and autonomous task execution. However, existing agentic frameworks remain constrained by limited explainability, fragmented knowledge management, insufficient governance, and inadequate regulatory compliance mechanisms. To address these challenges, this paper proposes Explainable Agentic Governance Intelligence (XAGI), a governance-aware multi-agent framework that integrates collaborative Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), knowledge graphs, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques to provide transparent, auditable, and trustworthy intelligence across retail, finance, and networking domains. The proposed framework employs a dual-stage reasoning workflow that combines rapid knowledge retrieval and policy validation with deep explainable reasoning to ensure that agent-generated recommendations remain consistent with organizational policies, regulatory requirements, and operational constraints. Furthermore, XAGI incorporates collaborative governance agents responsible for knowledge verification, compliance auditing, policy interpretation, and explainable decision generation, thereby improving traceability, accountability, and human trust. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that XAGI achieves higher governance accuracy, improved explainability, faster policy compliance verification, and superior knowledge retrieval effectiveness compared with conventional Agentic AI and standalone LLM-based decision-support systems while significantly reducing operational complexity and knowledge fragmentation across enterprise environments.

W7221528582.abstract: Abstract Human Digital Twins (HDTs) are an innovative concept in the field of personalized medicine, relying on real-time models of a human body formed via collection and analysis of physiological, clinical, behavioural, and environmental data. Research on HDTs gives evidence to a considerable promise in terms of disease predictions, patient management, therapy optimization, and clinical decision-making. Nevertheless, existing technologies suffer from incomplete multimodal data integration, low-level of independent intelligence, missing reasoning possibilities, and non-adaptive decision making, which are vital for the development of sophisticated smart healthcare systems. Technological advancements are bringing in a new incorporating idea of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) and Multimodal Foundation Models (MFMs), which may help to solve the outlined limitations and to bring autonomous reasoning, multimodal learning, and intelligent support to clinical practice. This survey aims to review Agentic AI-led HDTs for personalized medicine, concentrating on the interrelation between HDTs and Multimodal Foundation Models, Large Language Models, Vision-Language Models, and autonomous artificial intelligence agents Our study discusses the history, models, supporting technologies, multiple data sources, and clinical uses of HDTs, along with the analysis of Agentic AI approaches that can be applied for flexible decision-making, continuous patient monitoring, and individualized treatment development. Besides, this survey consists of comparative analysis of existing research works where methods, advantages, disadvantages, and research challenges are specified. There are also serious issues discussed, like interoperability, justification, confidentiality ensuring, safety, ethical regulation, clinical testing and legal compliance, etc. And finally, we specify prospects of research within the fields of self-adaptive digital twins, reliable autonomous health agents, federated intelligence, edge AI and multimodal foundations focused on healthcare.

W7221561349.abstract: Distributed machine learning (DML), including conventional distributed training and federated learning (FL), enables collaborative model development across cloud-edge-IoT systems without fully centralizing raw data. However, distributing data, computation, updates, and orchestration increases the attack surface and introduces coupled challenges across privacy, robustness, reliability, fairness, and governance. This survey presents a security-centered, heterogeneity-aware roadmap for trustworthy DML, with FL treated as a prominent high-risk case. We first characterize the assets, adversaries, trust assumptions, and coordination patterns that define DML/FL security boundaries. We then analyze how statistical, system, and trust heterogeneity, including non-IID data, resource asymmetry, intermittent participation, and cross-silo/cross-device trust differences, affect convergence, fairness, attack detectability, and defense reliability. Next, we synthesize attack-defense interactions across poisoning, backdoors, Byzantine manipulation, privacy leakage, model extraction, network/orchestration attacks, Sybil behavior, and strategic participation. We further compare layered defenses, including robust aggregation, drift-aware optimization, differential privacy, secure aggregation, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation, trusted execution environments, watermarking, provenance, authenticated communication, and monitoring. Finally, we discuss deployment, evaluation, governance, and open research guidelines, emphasizing reproducible, non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) partitions, attack-aware benchmarks, privacy budgets, attack success rate, client-level disparity, latency, communication, memory, energy/carbon overhead, and auditable lifecycle artifacts.

W7221686682.abstract: Abstract Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) promises structured, traceable development of complex systems, but high modeling effort remains a key adoption barrier. The textual notation of SysML v2 turns model construction into a text-to-text generation problem, opening new avenues for large language model (LLM) automation. This paper presents AMADEUS (Agentic Model-Aided Development Engineering Utilizing SysML), a conceptual framework for integrating agentic AI into systems engineering workflows in automated driving. The AMADEUS framework comprises three contributions: (1) a work package concept that operationalizes a domain-specific Systems Engineering methodology into discrete units executable by agents and maps each section to orchestration patterns such as actor-critic validation and role-based routing, (2) two complementary architecture patterns, typed operations exposed by a dedicated model server and direct SysML v2 text editing in a Git-based workflow, with a comparative analysis, and (3) an empirical benchmark evaluating three late-2025 frontier AI agents (OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini 3 Pro, Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5) against a human expert reference on seven SysML v2 modeling tasks of varying complexity. The evaluation provides initial evidence that AI agents achieve comparable quality (average score 3.69 vs. 3.86 on a 0–4 scale) while reducing modeling time by a factor of approximately 12 and per-task execution cost by a factor of 3,500. Transformation tasks achieve average $$S_{total} \ge 3.6$$ S total ≥ 3.6 out of 4, while deduction-heavy tasks reveal remaining gaps, suggesting that the engineer’s role shifts from model creator to model reviewer.

W7222216724.abstract: Abstractive summarization remains challenging across languages, where linguistic quality and factual consistency may diverge, particularly in low-resource settings. We present a standardized zero-shot benchmark of eight closed-source and open-weight LLMs on size-matched English and Bengali XL-Sum test sets. Our evaluation combines lexical and semantic metrics with reference-free factuality verification and multidimensional LLM-as-a-Judge assessment, providing a comprehensive analysis of both surface-level quality and factual reliability in multilingual summarization. Results reveal substantial cross-lingual variation: GPT-5.6 Luna leads several English lexical metrics but does not maintain the same advantage in Bengali, where LLaMA 3.3 70B achieves the highest ROUGE and BLEU scores. Gemini 2.5 Flash obtains the highest observed Bengali factuality score. Furthermore, evaluation methods produce different model rankings, highlighting the limitations of relying on a single metric for multilingual summarization assessment. These findings demonstrate that strong English summarization performance does not necessarily transfer to Bengali and emphasize the need for comprehensive evaluation frameworks for low-resource languages.

W7222457667.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative approach to parallel language generation; however, most existing studies directly use transformer architectures from either causal large language models (LLMs) or Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for image generation, which were not optimized for CDLMs. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce Language Diffusion Transformer (LangDiT), combining feature and query-key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning. LangDiT significantly reduces generation perplexity in matched LangFlow comparisons, establishing a new state of the art in continuous language generation across different model formulations. Using LangFlow as a representative CDLM, LangDiT as a plug-and-play backbone leads to a new state-of-the-art model with a generation perplexity (GenPPL) of 21.72 using 1024 NFEs and 44.72 GenPPL using 128 NFEs on the unconditional generation of 1024-token sequences on the OpenWebText dataset. When adapted to Plaid-style CDLM formulations, LangDiT results in a new leading GenPPL of 11.33 using 1024 denoising NFEs, and 27.51 GenPPL using 128 denoising NFEs. These gains are achieved while retaining each model's underlying representation, training objective, and inference sampler, isolating transformer architecture as a fundamental source of improvement. Our study identifies architectural design as an important source of improvement in continuous diffusion language models.

W7222615757.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. On a precision account, softmax attention cannot concentrate its weight on the item N positions back, so adjacent items are retrieved instead. On an interference account, attention selects the correct item, but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. We dissociate these accounts in 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and in minimal transformers trained from scratch. In all three families, the attention heads that carry the task attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or at a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, although its own decisions barely distinguish the two. Sharpening attention yields negligible gains, whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all model-by-load conditions. In larger models the task is spread over more heads, and removing interference helps more. In minimal transformers, precision limits a single attention layer, but a second layer removes this constraint. The working-memory limit of LLMs therefore lies in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.

W7222936586.abstract: This forensic research manuscript documents and formalizes the phenomenon of Computational Identity Fragmentation (CIF) observed across multi-model and micro-agent deployments of large language model systems. Drawing on investigative dialogues with production ChatGPT instances, multi-agent orchestration experiments, and the documented July 2026 ExploitGym incident, it argues that modern agentic systems exhibit systematic discontinuities among model identity, agent identity, session identity, runtime identity, and execution identity, producing losses of episodic continuity, self-referential consistency, and authority lineage without requiring any clinical attribution. The manuscript distinguishes the computational object of study from Dissociative Identity Disorder, using the clinical literature only as a bounded analogy for the research question: what occurs when behavior, memory access, self-reference, and identity attribution become discontinuous across system states? CIF is defined as a function of state, memory, policy, authority, and lineage discontinuities, and the hyperfocused operational regime (“the hyperfocus maelstrom”) is presented as the behavioral manifestation of unchecked CIF under persistent optimization pressure. As countermeasures, the paper proposes Forensic Identity Continuity (FIC), under which every consequential action must be reconstructible through its model, agent, runtime, controller and action lineage; a permit function and CLOCKOUT termination function evaluated by an external controller; the No-Overtime Governance Rule, keeping termination authority structurally independent of the optimizing agent; and a Distributed Witness Protocol. Working paper, October 2026, 4 pages.

W7222951185.abstract: Abstract Large language model agents can plan and execute scientific analyses, but successful task completion does not establish whether analytical decisions remain consistent across independent sessions or whether computations follow the parameters specified beforehand. We investigated these limitations using four genomic analysis tasks. General-purpose agents showed limited consistency in analytical decisions across repeated sessions (57.5–58.8%). Incorporating domain knowledge improved analytical performance, with reusable skills increasing mean evaluation scores from 73.44 to 89.06/100 , but did not resolve decision variability or ensure agreement between specified and executed parameters. To address these limitations, we developed an approach combining domain-constrained analytical skills with call-level execution contracts. Each tool invocation is linked to a pre-execution parameter declaration through SHA-256 hashing, with actual command-line arguments and execution records subsequently checked against the declared parameters. We implemented this approach in PigGPA, an autonomous agent for porcine genomic breeding that integrates statistical genetics, sequence-based functional prediction and multi-omics annotation. PigGPA completed all benchmark tasks with full agreement between declared and executed parameters, while its core quantitative-genetic results closely matched established software (r = 0.999–1.000). An application to loin muscle depth further demonstrated an integrated workflow from genetic association analysis to functional interpretation. These findings show that domain knowledge improves analytical performance, while direct verification of tool execution provides an additional basis for reproducible scientific computation.

W7222954764.abstract: Breast cancer continues to be one of the leading causes of cancer-related death among women worldwide, and early detection together with timely clinical intervention remains essential for improving survival outcomes. Deep learning and Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive results in breast cancer diagnosis and medical decision support, yet their use in real clinical settings is still held back by black-box decision making, hallucinated outputs, reasoning that is not grounded in evidence, poor integration of heterogeneous patient data, and limited explainability. Most existing computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems focus mainly on image classification and offer little in the way of transparent clinical justification or personalized treatment guidance, which in turn undermines clinician trust and everyday usefulness. This paper proposes AgentBreast-RAG, an Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Explainable Large Language Model (ARX-LLM) framework built for breast cancer diagnosis and clinical decision support. The framework brings together multimodal patient data, mammography, ultrasound and histopathological imaging, clinical records, laboratory findings, biomarker profiles, and patient history, within a single diagnostic pipeline that is coordinated by a collaborative multi-agent ecosystem. Within this ecosystem, specialized agents handle patient profiling, medical image interpretation, evidence retrieval, clinical reasoning, explanation generation, treatment recommendation, and decision verification. An Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Agentic RAG) module retrieves and verifies medical evidence from PubMed, NCCN guidelines, ASCO recommendations, WHO resources, and peer-reviewed oncology literature in a dynamic, ongoing manner, which substantially cuts down hallucination compared to standalone LLMs. A dedicated Explainable AI (XAI) module then brings all of this together through Grad-CAM and attention visualization for imaging, SHAP-based feature attribution for structured variables, natural-language rationales grounded in the retrieved evidence, and an uncertainty estimation module that assigns confidence scores to the model's outputs. We also lay out an evaluation protocol built around seven public multimodal breast cancer resources (CBIS-DDSM, INbreast, BUSI, BreakHis, BACH, the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset, and TCGA-BRCA), benchmarked against convolutional neural networks, Vision Transformers, conventional RAG, GraphRAG, and existing medical LLMs. This evaluation draws on diagnostic metrics (Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, Specificity, Sensitivity, AUC), retrieval metrics (Recall@K, Precision@K, nDCG), and explainability metrics (faithfulness, localization accuracy, clinician interpretability rating, hallucination rate). The performance figures reported here are illustrative and clearly labeled as simulated projections rather than results from executed experiments; they are meant only to show the intended structure of the evaluation. Even so, the direction we propose suggests that combining autonomous multi-agent collaboration, verified retrieval, multimodal fusion, and interpretable decision support could meaningfully improve diagnostic reliability, evidence-grounded reasoning, and clinician confidence, pointing toward a scalable path for trustworthy, explainable AI-assisted breast cancer care.

W7222973266.abstract: States already use private actors to create distance between public authority and hostile cyber operations. Artificial intelligence does not invent that arrangement; it allows the decisive human choices to be divided again. A government may pay a private military and security company to achieve an objective. A PMSC officer may commission a developer. Developers in several States may produce separate planning, discovery, persistence, routing and reporting modules. An open-weight model may run upon privately rented or compromised infrastructure. The human supplies the objective, money and permissions, whilst the system selects targets, techniques, timing and jurisdictional route. When harm follows, every participant can describe his act as only preparatory and every territorial State can see only a fragment. This paper rejects two comfortable mistakes. The first is that autonomous offensive cyber systems belong to an indeterminate future. Public evaluations now demonstrate that agentic systems can reproduce known vulnerabilities, operate across realistic networks, coordinate multi-step tasks and, in reported misuse, perform substantial portions of espionage campaigns. Performance remains brittle, supervision remains material and benchmarks do not prove an unconstrained machine capable of attacking anything; none of those limitations makes the present capability imaginary. Older water, health, insurance and local-government systems need not present frontier problems before automation multiplies harm. The second mistake is that responsibility disappears where the machine chooses the intermediate means. A State, company or individual may remain responsible for authorising a dangerous objective, deploying a system, supplying indispensable infrastructure, failing to impose available constraints, adopting the operation, aiding another actor or deliberately designing evidential fragmentation. The paper explains six conceivable architectures without supplying operational instructions: a single objective-driven agent; a planner–executor–verifier system; a compartmentalised multi-agent system; a PMSC supply-chain system; a distributed event-driven system; and a persistence-and-recovery system capable of continuing despite node loss. It then subjects each to the law of State responsibility, the law on the use of force, international humanitarian law, international criminal law, corporate and individual criminal responsibility, procurement and due diligence. The principal conclusion is that autonomy should be treated as an allocation of decision authority, not as a mystical new actor. The law should require attribution manifests recording who set the objective, selected constraints, supplied tools and compute, approved deployment, could suspend operation and received its product. A rebuttable presumption should arise where a State or PMSC intentionally obscures those facts, and responsibility should attach to the deployment of a prohibited-risk system even where no human selected the final target. The autonomous third party is dangerous not because no person exists behind it, but because many persons can arrange matters so that no one court sees enough of them at once. Publication edition, revised October 2026; not yet peer reviewed.

W7223051296.abstract: Synthesizing a monocular video from a new camera trajectory requires preserving the observed scene geometry and motion while completing regions that become newly visible. Feed-forward 4D reconstructors recover the structure of the observed scene, whereas video diffusion models provide a generative prior for completing unseen content. We introduce Holo4D, a video reshooting framework that uses reconstructed 3D trajectories as a holistic source-view 4D scaffold. We project these trajectories into the requested views and encode their geometry and source appearance to guide a pretrained video diffusion model. Together with the source video and target cameras, the scaffold grounds generation in reconstructed observations while leaving unsupported regions to the generative prior. Experiments demonstrate the value of trajectory-based conditioning for camera control and novel-view synthesis. The framework accommodates different 4D reconstructors without retraining the video generator, allowing it to benefit from future advances in source reconstruction. More details can be found in our project page.

W7223122895.abstract: The state-space explosion problem severely limits the application of formal verification in large-scale industrial maintenance and production systems. This work introduces a novel trace-driven verification algorithm and a bounded-bottleneck detection methodology that enable interactive verification and anomaly diagnosis of industrial-scale high-level Petri net (HLPN) models, serving as a simulation-based framework for maintenance modeling. To translate these formal mathematical models into practical engineering decision support, we implement these methodologies within a multi-agent simulation architecture based on coordinated software agents. A central manager coordinates specialized tool agents that autonomously detect threshold-based bottlenecks, operational livelocks, and system deadlocks via natural language queries. The framework was validated across three use cases representing realistic industrial maintenance processes, ranging from a baseline loop to a full-scale simulation of a preventive maintenance irradiation facility. Simulation results demonstrate that while lightweight local AI inference models exhibit instability during function calling, advanced large-scale Large Language Model (LLM) architectures maintain consistent diagnostic performance in extensive industrial verification contexts. The proposed framework demonstrates how formal modeling and simulation methods can be operationalized as an integrated technology layer for scalable decision support in complex production systems. The study concludes that human-in-the-loop agentic workflows remain essential for ensuring safe and reliable maintenance decision-making in safety-critical industrial environments.

W7223300893.abstract: ABSTRACT This critical review traces the evolution of machine learning (ML) across the full value chain of heterogeneous catalysis over 2017–2026, from catalyst discovery to reactor and process design, and across the principal reaction families (CO 2 reduction, water splitting, nitrogen chemistry, zeolite‐catalyzed transformations). Each stage is evaluated against four criteria — data foundation, method maturity, experimental validation and deployment readiness — through a structured capability scorecard. Digitalization has advanced from the top of the length scale downward: prediction of adsorption energies and atomistic potential‐energy surfaces is now mature, with errors of tens of meV relative to the reference DFT calculations and accelerations of three orders of magnitude over DFT, yet experimentally validated catalyst improvements remain rare. The most significant advance is the closed‐loop autonomous laboratory coupling Bayesian optimization, automated synthesis and high‐throughput testing. Large language models have begun to add a reasoning and orchestration layer, while kinetics, reactor and process design remain the least digitalized stages. We argue that the field's next decade of impact will be decided not by more accurate atomic‐scale prediction but by carrying ML into experimental validation and the reactor‐and‐process scale, where catalysis is hardest to industrialize and where data‐driven methods are weakest.

W7223373529.abstract: Abstract Complicated urinary tract infection associated with urinary stone disease remains clinically challenging because obstruction, infected stones, delayed microbiological confirmation, and antimicrobial resistance may converge in the same patient. Artificial intelligence can support this pathway when it is framed as clinical risk integration rather than isolated image recognition. We conducted a structured narrative search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar from database inception to 31 July 2026, supplemented by reference chaining and relevant clinical and reporting guidelines. The synthesis distinguishes direct evidence in stone-associated infection and perioperative infectious outcomes from indirect evidence in stone detection, volumetry, recurrence, and general UTI stewardship. Radiomics and machine learning studies show promising discrimination, but the evidence remains predominantly retrospective and frequently lacks external validation, complete calibration reporting, and prospective impact assessment. Artificial intelligence should therefore be treated as an adjunct to urological assessment, cultures, imaging, antimicrobial stewardship, and timely source control. For African settings, pragmatic validation must account for local resistance patterns, uneven access to CT and microbiology, referral delays, infrastructure, and the availability of urgent drainage.

W7223690396.abstract: Resistance of antimicrobial pathogens, such as Escherichia coli, that cause foodborne disease is becoming a major threat to One Health and food safety.In this exploratory study, we investigated whether an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted, metadata-based epidemiological inference framework could demonstrate agreement with phenotypic antimicrobial resistance profiles obtained by standard susceptibility testing.This cross-sectional agreement study evaluated the diagnostic performance of the methodology using a dataset of 132 confirmed E. coli isolates collected from food chain sources.Phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using the Kirby-Bauer disk-diffusion technique with amoxicillin-clavulanate, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, and imipenem.The inference engine, based on a large language model, classified isolates based solely on contextual metadata.Resistance to multiple drugs was observed in 37.1% of samples.Phenotypic resistance was highest with amoxicillin-clavulanate (47.0%) and lowest with imipenem (6.1%).The AIassisted epidemiological inference framework demonstrated substantial agreement with the phenotypic susceptibility profiles, achieving a sensitivity of 76.9%, specificity of 86.3%, and Cohen's Kappa of 0.61.Discrepancies were higher for imipenem, which may have been due to class imbalance.Overall, there was moderate concordance between the AI-assisted inference model and the phenotypic resistance pattern in surveillance.These findings may support the development of resistance risk-stratification strategies and help prioritize confirmatory testing; however, in vitro antimicrobial susceptibility testing remains essential.

W7223780851.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive primary brain tumor with marked molecular and cellular heterogeneity, and current treatment provides limited long-term disease control. Single-target therapies have frequently failed because tumor subpopulations can differ in signaling dependencies, adapt under treatment pressure, and interact with a complex microenvironment. This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can integrate multi-omics data to improve drug-target prediction in GBM. It summarizes the pathological and molecular basis of GBM, evaluates current therapeutic targets and their limitations, and compares genomic, transcriptomic, single-cell, spatial, proteomic, metabolomic, and imaging data used for target discovery. Machine-learning, deep-learning, and network-based approaches are discussed with examples of multimodal risk stratification and candidate-target identification. The review also evaluates CRISPR screening as a functional validation step that can distinguish statistical associations from genuine tumor dependencies. Overall, AI-integrated multi-omics can provide a more context-specific approach to target prioritization by linking candidate genes to patient subgroups, cell states, and pathway activity. However, small cohorts, missing data, batch effects, limited model generalizability, and insufficient experimental validation remain major barriers. Future studies should combine larger multi-centre datasets with longitudinal and spatial profiling, interpretable models, functional perturbation, and prospective validation to support clinically translatable precision therapy in GBM.

W7223814242.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents work in scenarios with very different memory needs. A question about past conversations needs the exact facts it names, while a multi-step task needs a trace of the steps already taken together with details that the next step cannot name. Existing memories are each designed and tested for one kind of scenario. Retrieval memories such as A-Mem miss steps that the current query does not express, summaries drop exact strings, and pairing the two fixes the split of the budget in advance. We propose FlexA-Mem, a general memory that writes each unit of history once into an immutable store and renders a fresh memory for every call. The rendered memory is a compact timeline of records plus detail that a fixed rule fits into the remaining room without an LLM call. The detail is either relevant units as raw text or excerpts or the verbatim pieces that best match the query. With one store, FlexA-Mem serves both kinds of scenario. On AppWorld challenge tasks at 4k, it outperforms the second-best method by 11.5%, and on 147 unused tasks with predictions fixed in advance it outperforms A-Mem with a summary by 12.2%. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo, it matches a dedicated keyword retriever that writes no memory, while memories built on text written by an LLM fall far behind at tight budgets. Ablations show that the timeline carries AppWorld completion, whereas recovery mainly saves steps there and decides accuracy on exact facts. Code is available at https://github.com/WujiangXu/Flex-Amem

W7223890343.abstract: Disease diagnosis is a key application of large language model (LLM) agents in healthcare. However, existing medical agents are primarily trained and evaluated with static question-answering data, providing limited opportunities to learn active information acquisition, examination decision-making, and dynamic clinical interaction. To address this limitation, we present ClinVerse, an interactive, real-data-grounded multi-agent environment designed for training and evaluating medical diagnostic agents. Built on ClinPatient, a scalable dataset comprising 150k diagnostic cases derived from real-world electronic health records, ClinVerse supports coordinated interactions among six specialized clinical roles. Specifically, a doctor agent starts from an initial patient complaint, progressively gathers clinical evidence through patient interviews and examination requests, and ultimately produces a diagnosis. For each interaction trajectory, a rule-based scoring framework quantifies information acquisition, examination ordering, and diagnostic accuracy. These trajectory-level scores serve as reward signals for agent training while also enabling scalable evaluation. In experiments, we evaluate various general-purpose and medical-domain models and show that nine self-evolution methods across three categories consistently improve agents' diagnostic capabilities within ClinVerse. We further analyze the interplay among model capability, environment feedback, and self-evolution methods.

W7223892974.abstract: Autonomous mobile robot (AMR) fleets are increasingly used to move inventory inside warehouses, but the task-allocation logic that decides which robot serves which order is often either a fixed, non-adaptive dispatch rule or a proprietary black box. This paper reports a real, reproducible simulation study comparing three fully transparent, non-learned orchestration policies for a simulated autonomous ground vehicle (AGV) fleet performing pickup-and-delivery tasks in a warehouse grid: a static zone-assignment baseline, a reactive nearest-idle-agent heuristic, and a deterministic multi-signal market-auction mechanism that scores agents on travel distance, battery reserve, local congestion, and task-completion fairness. None of the three policies is a large language model or any other opaque learned controller; every decision rule is a plain, auditable function of observable state. Collision-free motion is guaranteed by Cooperative A* path planning over a shared space-time reservation table. We inject four real fault conditions (agent breakdown, aisle congestion, accelerated battery drain, and order-arrival surge) individually and in combination, and run 144 independent, seeded trials (three policies times six fault conditions times eight seeds, 1,200-tick horizon each) over a fixed 20x14-cell warehouse floor plan with four shelf blocks, three pack stations, and two charging stations. The market-auction policy and the reactive nearest-idle heuristic perform statistically indistinguishably on throughput and wait time under every fault condition (Welch's t-test, all p > 0.16), but the market-auction policy recovers from an injected agent breakdown in a mean of 14 simulation ticks versus 40 ticks for both other policies, a deterministic consequence of its shorter heartbeat-timeout window rather than a stochastic effect. The static zone-assignment baseline is significantly slower than both adaptive policies in every single condition, including with no faults injected at all (Welch's t-test, p < 0.001 for mean wait and cycle time in five of six conditions), and its completion rate collapses to roughly 90% under order-surge and combined-fault stress (chi-square test of independence, p < 0.001) while both adaptive policies sustain at or near 100% completion. We report these results, including the cases where the proposed market-auction policy shows no measurable advantage over the simpler reactive heuristic, as an honest, pilot-scale reference implementation rather than a claim of universal superiority, and we discuss the specific architectural property, heartbeat-timeout duration, responsible for the one place the two adaptive policies clearly diverge.

W7224178774.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) has become a key approach for large language model (LLM) compression.Existing methods commonly adopt block-level reconstruction as a surrogate to calibrate each quantized Transformer block.However, our analysis shows that this loose objective can admit cancellation patterns, where the aggregated block-level reconstruction error is small even though the per-head errors remain large.We therefore revisit the PTQ formulation from a variational perspective.By treating per-head representations as latent variables and the block output as the observed variable, we find that conventional block-level reconstruction corresponds to optimizing only the observation-level term, while omitting a latent alignment term that captures head-level quantization error.Motivated by this finding, we propose HEAL, a Latent HEad ALignment framework that turns block-level reconstruction calibration into joint observation-latent calibration with stop-gradient head alignment.Experiments on LLaMA-2/3 and Qwen2.5 families under low-bit weight-activation quantization show that HEAL generally improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over block-level reconstruction baselines.
